5e4bbcb8c65563d4: Assistant robot architecture: a microphone and Whisper turn speech into text; the language model chooses actions from a fixed list; the validator checks the plan; the executors control the SO-101 arm and mobile base; the camera checks the object; the emergency stop cuts the power independently of all software.
a2425c64b0668975: Grasp with verification: the camera checks whether the object is on the table; if it isn’t, the robot alerts you and stops; if it is, the policy picks it up; then the camera checks whether the object has left the table; if it hasn’t, the robot tries once more and then gives up and alerts you.
dfc3bc10dccffe88: Complete robot wiring: the computer communicates by USB with the SO-101 arm and over serial with the base’s ESP32; the ESP32 controls the H-bridge and motors; the arm’s battery and the base’s battery are separate, with a shared GND for the logic and an emergency stop button that cuts power to both.
2029ca30c62bb240: Chain success: starting with 20 requests, 18 are heard correctly, 16 become valid plans, 13 result in the object being picked up, and 12 are delivered; the bar that drops the most shows which step needs improvement—in this case, the grasp.
db34506bb6c170d8: Final course project: an assistant robot that listens, plans using a language model within a fixed list of actions, sees, picks up objects with the SO-101 arm, and moves on a mobile base, with testing, metrics, and documentation.

b57a6819e2ace941: Three motors side by side: the DC motor spins continuously and controls speed; the servo moves to an angle between 0 and 180 degrees and holds its position; the stepper motor moves in equal steps and keeps track of how many it has taken.
02187d7450cdb324: An H-bridge with four switches, S1 to S4, around motor M. With S1 and S4 closed, current flows through the motor from left to right and it turns forward. With S2 and S3 closed, current flows the other way and it turns backward.
b3266e9b8a6ab4e6: Three PWM signals with the same voltage level: at a 25 percent duty cycle, the TT motor is in the dead zone and doesn't turn; at 50 percent it turns at half speed; at 90 percent it runs close to maximum speed.
768473c5f60bc096: Servo pulses: a pulse arrives every 20 milliseconds. A 0.5 millisecond pulse moves the arm to 0 degrees, a 1.5 millisecond pulse to 90 degrees, and a 2.4 millisecond pulse to 180 degrees.
1531f85cca286200: Battery comparison by the current they can deliver: a 9-volt rectangular battery delivers very little and isn't suitable for a motor; 4 AA NiMH batteries deliver enough to get started; two 18650 cells with BMS deliver plenty; a 2S LiPo delivers a lot, but requires more care.
69b4f0bc39e6d934: Rover power distribution: the battery passes through the switch and splits into two branches. One goes to the driver's VM, which powers the motors through capacitors. The other passes through the 5-volt buck converter and powers the ESP32, the HC-SR04, and the servo. The ESP32's 3V3 powers the driver's logic. All GND connections meet at a common point.

MEETING PLAN · Track 1
Course modules: 1.1 (topic 6) and 1.4 (topic 2)
Today's goal: each group sees the LED blink and the distance in cm in the Serial Monitor.

1. OPENING
   Question: "how does a robot vacuum know the wall is close?"
   Show a bat or a car's reverse sensor: sound that bounces back.

2. DEMONSTRATION
   On the projector: the 1.1 blinking LED running in Wokwi (GPIO 2, 220-ohm resistor).
   Then the HC-SR04 in Wokwi: drag the distance control and watch the number change.

3. HANDS-ON
   a) Wokwi: copy the 1.1 blinking LED, assemble the circuit, press play.
   b) Real kit: build the same circuit on the breadboard and upload with Arduino IDE 2.x.
   c) Connect the HC-SR04: VCC to 5 V, GND to GND, Trig to a GPIO,
      Echo through the voltage divider to another GPIO (see module 1.4).
   d) Copy the code from module 1.4 and open the Serial Monitor.
   It worked when: your hand at 10 cm shows as about 10 on the monitor.
   Expected errors: charge-only cable, reversed LED, Echo without a voltage divider,
   Serial Monitor baud rate different from the one in the code.

4. CHALLENGE
   The LED turns on when something is less than 20 cm away (combine the two code examples).

5. RECORD
   Logbook + short video of the LED reacting to your hand.

Safety for today: never put 5 V on an ESP32 input pin;
disconnect USB before changing wires.

MEETING PLAN · Track 3
Course module: 3.3 Detect objects with YOLO26
Goal for the day: each group measures when the detector gets it right and when it gets it wrong.

BEFORE (teacher): Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit, virtual environment
created and the package already installed (pip install ultralytics), model
yolo26n downloaded, camera tested. Installing it during the meeting won’t work.

1. OPENING
   Question: "what does the robot need to know to follow a person?"
   Connection: in 3.2 the camera found a color; today it recognizes objects.

2. DEMONSTRATION
   Run the module 3.3 example on the Pi 5 with the camera pointed at the room.
   Show the boxes, the class name, and the confidence score.

3. HANDS-ON (each group tests and fills in the table)
   Objects: bottle, phone, cup, one person from the group.
   For each one: good light / dim light · near / far · from the side.
   Record: detected? what confidence? did anything appear that wasn’t there?
   Success criteria: the group has at least 12 test rows.

4. CHALLENGE
   Export to NCNN and compare the speed, as in module 3.3:
   yolo export model=yolo26n.pt format=ncnn
   How many images per second before and after?

5. LOG
   Logbook + the test table + one conclusion:
   "under what conditions should our robot NOT trust the camera?"

Safety for the day: Pi 5 with a cooler and official power supply;
do not connect or disconnect the camera while the Pi is powered.
